title: Relative clauses 3: whose/whom/where
subtitle: whose car / whom I met / where I grew up
summary: Use whose for possession, whom as a formal object pronoun for people, and where for places in relative clauses.

lesson.heading: whose
lesson.text: When we were driving home, we saw some people standing by the road. Their car had broken down, so we stopped to help them: *We helped some people **whose car had broken down**.* **Whose** replaces *his / her / their* and is used mostly for people.

examples.text: A widow is a woman **whose husband** is dead.
I met someone **whose brother** I went to school with.
examples.note: I went to school with his or her brother

examples.text: This school is only for children **whose first language** is not English.

left.label: who
examples: I met a man **who** knows you.
I met a couple **who** have just got married.
I met a man **who** owns a restaurant.

right.label: whose
examples: I met a man **whose** sister knows you.
I met somebody **whose** mother writes detective stories.
I met somebody **whose** parents used to work in a circus.

lesson.heading: whose is not who's
lesson.text: **Whose** and **who's** sound the same, but **who's** = *who is* or *who has*.

examples.text: I have a friend **who's** learning Arabic.
I have a friend **who's** just started learning Arabic.
I have a friend **whose** sister is learning Arabic.

lesson.heading: whom
lesson.text: **Whom** is possible instead of *who* when it is the **object** of the verb. You can also use a preposition + whom. Whom is formal and we rarely use it in spoken English.

examples.text: George is a person **whom I admire** very much.
It's important to have friends **with whom** you can relax.
Less formal: a person **I admire** a lot, or friends **you can relax with**.

lesson.heading: where
lesson.text: We use **where** in a relative clause to talk about a place.

examples.text: I recently went back to the town **where I grew up**.
The restaurant **where we had lunch** was near the airport.
I would like to live in a place **where there is** plenty of sunshine.
A cemetery is a place **where people are buried**.

lesson.heading: the day, the time, the reason
lesson.text: We say *the day we got married*, *the year I was born*, *the last time they met*, *the reason I'm calling you* - with no relative pronoun at all. You can also add **that**.

examples.text: I can't meet you on Friday. That's **the day I'm going away**.
**The last time I saw** her, she looked great.
examples.note: or The last time that I saw her ...

examples.text: **The reason I'm calling** you is to ask your advice.
examples.note: or The reason that / why I'm calling you ...

lesson.text: Whose is always followed by a noun (whose car, whose name); where is followed by a complete clause with no missing object.

exercises.prompt: We helped some people ___ car had broken down.
exercises.explanation: Their car had broken down, so we use whose + noun.

exercises.prompt: I met a man ___ sister knows you.
exercises.explanation: His sister knows you, so we need whose (possession), not who.

exercises.prompt: Match each word with its definition.

pairs.right: a woman whose husband is dead
a child whose parents are dead
a person who believes that all wars are wrong
a place where people are buried
a place where everybody knows everybody else

exercises.prompt: What's the name of the hotel ___ your parents are staying?
exercises.explanation: A hotel is a place, so we use where.

exercises.prompt: This school is only for children ___ first language is not English.
exercises.explanation: Their first language is not English, so we use whose.

exercises.prompt: I have a friend ___ just started learning Arabic.
exercises.explanation: Who's = who has here. Whose would need a noun after it.

exercises.prompt: At a party you met a person and her mother writes detective stories. Tell a friend about it.
exercises.answer: I met somebody whose mother writes detective stories
exercises.explanation: Whose replaces her: her mother writes detective stories.

exercises.prompt: At the party I met a couple ___ just got married.
exercises.explanation: The couple have just got married - the relative pronoun is the subject, so we use who.

exercises.statement: George is a person whom I admire very much.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Whom is the object of admire, so it is possible here (though who or nothing is more usual in speech).

exercises.prompt: The person from ___ I bought my car is a friend of my father's.
exercises.explanation: After a preposition we use whom, not who.

exercises.statement: The person to who I spoke wasn't very helpful.
exercises.explanation: The person to whom I spoke wasn't very helpful (or, less formally, The person I spoke to wasn't very helpful).

exercises.prompt: The last time ___ her, she looked great.
exercises.explanation: After the last time we need no relative pronoun at all - or we can add that.
